Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool today called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS**. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting the right support.  

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. When you’re ready, we’ll go through one question at a time; it usually takes only a few minutes.  

Let’s start:  

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft voice, slow breathing]  
"Mostly… I haven’t really laughed much at all. It feels hard to find anything funny right now."
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Postpartum Mental Health Professional: Thank you. Next question: Over the past week, have you looked forward with enjoyment to things, or has that been difficult.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
"Sometimes I still get a little excited about my favorite show or a short walk, but it’s nowhere near how I used to feel. Most things just seem kind of flat—like I’m going through the motions."
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

"Yes... whenever the baby fusses for a long time or I can’t soothe him right away, I catch myself thinking I’m doing something wrong as a mom. I know it’s probably not completely my fault, yet I still blame myself anyway."
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
“Yes… some days I feel anxious without warning—tight chest, racing thoughts—even when nothing’s wrong. It’s like my body just switches on the worry, and I can’t find the off button.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week I’ve suddenly felt really scared—heart pounding, can’t catch my breath—even though nothing bad was happening. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s awful while it’s going on.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly notice the pile of laundry or dishes, and it feels like too much. I usually manage to get through it, but I’m exhausted and on edge the whole time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Yes… I lie down exhausted, yet I can’t switch off. Thoughts just keep looping—baby’s breathing, tomorrow’s chores, did I do enough today? Takes me ages, then I wake at every small cry.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes… it’s like a heavy sadness hangs over me. I feel tearful for stretches—sometimes half the day—and it doesn’t lift much, even when I tell myself I should feel better.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… sometimes I just start crying without warning—maybe two or three times this week. Yesterday I cried while folding laundry; the tears come and I can’t stop them, even though nothing big triggered them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
A scary thought did pop up briefly—like a flash of “what if I weren’t here” when the nights feel endless. I’d never act on it; I love my baby, yet the thought has surfaced once or twice this week.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: ## Screening Summary – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety  
*(not a formal diagnosis – for clinical risk-flagging only)*

### Identified Symptoms / Patterns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia (“things seem pointless”)  
- Marked guilt/self-blame when baby fusses  
- Episodic panic-type anxiety (rapid onset, no trigger)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine chores  
- Frequent crying spells, difficulty falling/staying asleep  
- Fleeting passive suicidal ideation (“what if I weren’t here”) ➔ safety risk flag

### Risk Factors  
- Sleep deprivation + guilt → mood spiral  
- Loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities  
- High maternal self-criticism  
- Passive suicidal thought (no plan, no intent) – needs safety plan discussion

### Clinical Notes  
- Edinburgh ≥ probable clinical cutoff; consider formal EPDS & PHQ-9  
- Provide crisis line / perinatal mental-health referral  
- Discuss supports: partner, family, home-help, lactation consultant  
- Re-screen in 1 week or sooner if symptoms worsen or any new suicidal ideation  

### Next Steps  
- Schedule provider visit / warm-hand-off to OB/maternal-mental-health team  
- Safety-planning sheet given; emergency numbers reviewed  
- Follow-up appointment booked
